About the simulation

Explore hydrogen spectral lines in the Bohr model, where energy levels follow En = −13.6/n² eV. Switch between emission (photon emitted) and absorption (photon absorbed) transitions.

Visuals
  • Left: quantized energy levels with transition arrows and labels.
  • Right: atom view with circular orbits and the moving electron.
  • Bottom: a log wavelength strip from 50 nm to 2500 nm (UV · visible · IR). Solid lines are visible wavelengths, dashed lines UV or IR. Transitions past 2500 nm (5 → 4, 6 → 4, 6 → 5, 7 → 5, 7 → 6) are flagged at the right edge rather than drawn at a wavelength they do not have.
  • Orbit rings are equally spaced so every jump stays watchable; the true Bohr radii grow as rn = n²a0.
Controls
  • Set transition levels with From n and To n.
  • Toggle Emission/Absorption mode — it mirrors the level pair, so the same λ lights up bright or goes dark.
  • Absorption starts from the level in From n, and the atom must already be there: cold hydrogen sits in n = 1 and absorbs only Lyman. Stellar Balmer absorption needs gas hot enough to hold atoms in n = 2.
  • Use the series buttons (Lyman, Balmer, Paschen) to fire every line of one series.
  • Adjust animation speed and clear recorded lines.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Look before you fire

Left: the Bohr ladder. Right: orbits. Bottom: an empty wavelength strip (UV · visible · IR). Mode is Emission; From n = 3, To n = 1.

Press Next when you have the layout, then predict where the line will land.

2 · Predict — where does 3 → 1 land?

You are about to emit a photon for the jump 3 → 1. Where on the strip will the line appear?

3 · Fire 3 → 1

Press Make Transition. Watch the electron drop and a mark appear on the strip. Read Last transition: region and λ.

Does the line sit in the visible rainbow, or off to the UV side?

4 · Why Lyman is invisible

Every Lyman line lands on n = 1. Those gaps are the largest, so every Lyman photon is ultraviolet. The colours you see from hydrogen are Balmer lines — jumps that land on n = 2 (3 → 2 is 656 nm red).

On the strip, UV and IR lines are drawn dashed: real photons your eye simply cannot register.

5 · Predict — absorption of 1 → 3

Mode is now Absorption. For the electron to climb 1 → 3, the absorbed photon must…

6 · Same gap, two arrows

Emission releases a photon; absorption swallows one. For a given pair of levels both carry the same energy, so both sit at the same wavelength: 1/λ = R (1/n₁² − 1/n₂²), with n₁ the lower level, n₂ the upper, R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹.

Flip the Mode switch and fire again — the wavelength that lit up bright now goes dark. Series are named by the lower level: Lyman n = 1, Balmer n = 2, Paschen n = 3.

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A hydrogen atom can sit only at certain energies. When its electron jumps from one level to another, the atom gives out or takes in a single photon. The sim shows the jump, then records that photon as a line on a wavelength strip.

What you'll learn

  • How the energy levels of hydrogen are set by the whole number n.
  • How the gap between two levels fixes the wavelength of the photon.
  • How the same jump shows up as an emission line or an absorption line.
The apparatus: an energy ladder (left), the atom with its orbits (middle) and the wavelength strip (bottom).

What's on screen

  • Energy ladder, left: seven levels, n = 1 to 7, each labelled in eV, with a dashed red line at E = 0 above them.
  • Atom view, middle: seven circular orbits and the moving electron. The rings are evenly spaced, not to scale.
  • Wavelength strip, bottom: 50 to 2500 nm. A solid line is visible light, a dashed line is ultraviolet or infrared.
See itStart from the default setup. Watch for: the ladder, the seven rings, and an empty strip with its UV, visible and IR bands.

03

The allowed energies of hydrogen are Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV, and the levels crowd together as n grows

In the Bohr model the electron can occupy only certain levels, numbered by the whole number n, the principal quantum number. Level n has the energy

Eₙ = −13.6 / n² eV
n = 1, 2, 3, …

The minus sign means the electron is bound: energy must be given to the atom to free it. Energy rises towards E = 0, the ionisation limit (n → ∞), so n = 1 is the lowest level, the ground state. The steps between neighbouring levels shrink as n rises, so the ladder bunches up below E = 0. The sim draws levels n = 1 to 7.

n1234567
Eₙ (eV)−13.60−3.40−1.51−0.85−0.54−0.38−0.28
See itRead the labels on the energy ladder. Watch for: n = 1 far below the rest, and the upper levels packed together just under E = 0.
04

A jump between two levels gives one photon whose energy is the whole gap

When the electron drops from an upper level to a lower one, the atom releases one photon that carries the whole energy difference. For a photon, ΔE = hf = hc/λ, so the gap fixes the wavelength:

ΔE = 13.6 (1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) eV
λ = hc/ΔE ≈ 1240 nm·eV / ΔE
n₁ is the lower level, n₂ the upper. The frequency is f = ΔE/h.
  • A bigger gap gives a shorter wavelength, and a smaller gap a longer one.
  • The sim calls a wavelength below 380 nm ultraviolet, 380 to 780 nm visible and above 780 nm infrared.
  • As a check on the arithmetic, a 2.0 eV photon has λ = 1240 / 2.0 = 620 nm, which the sim calls orange.
05

Lines are grouped by the level they end on: Lyman lines are ultraviolet, Balmer lines visible and Paschen lines infrared

A series is every jump that ends on one lower level. The sim runs three, with n up to 7:

SeriesEnds onLinesWavelengthsRegion
Lymann = 16122 to 93 nmultraviolet
Balmern = 25656 to 397 nmvisible
Paschenn = 341876 to 1005 nminfrared

Every Lyman jump releases at least 10.2 eV, far more than any Balmer jump (at most 3.12 eV) or Paschen jump (at most 1.23 eV). So 3 → 1 gives a Lyman line at about 103 nm. Of all the jumps between the seven levels, only the five Balmer lines are visible. The jump 3 → 2 is red, at about 656 nm, 4 → 2 is blue, and the other three are violet.

The same results follow from the Rydberg form, 1/λ = R (1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) with R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹.

From n To n

These boxes move the sim's From n and To n. They do not fire a jump.

See itFire the jump 3 → 1. Watch for: a dashed line left of the visible band, and the readout showing about 103 nm and Ultraviolet.
See itRun the Balmer series. Watch for: five solid lines inside the visible band, from violet on the left to red on the right.
06

Absorption removes the same wavelengths that emission adds, but only from a level the atom already occupies

Absorption is the reverse jump. The electron climbs from a lower level to a higher one by swallowing a photon whose energy is exactly that gap. So 1 → 3 absorption takes the same ΔE, and the same wavelength, that 3 → 1 emission gives out. The Mode toggle swaps From n and To n so you can compare the two.

In absorption mode the strip shows a continuous band of colour, standing for white light, with a black line at each wavelength the atom has removed.

  • The photon energy must match a gap. In this model a photon that matches no gap passes through. A photon above 13.6 eV on an atom in n = 1 would free the electron, which the sim leaves out.
  • The atom must already be in the lower level. Cold hydrogen sits in n = 1, so it absorbs only Lyman lines.
  • Balmer absorption, as seen in stars, needs gas hot enough to hold atoms in n = 2.
See itSwitch to Absorption and fire 1 → 3. Watch for: one black line on the continuous band, at about 103 nm, the wavelength of the 3 → 1 emission line.
07

The strip covers 50 to 2500 nm, so some jumps are flagged at the edge instead of drawn

The strip's axis is logarithmic, which gives each decade of wavelength the same room. Five jumps between the upper levels have wavelengths beyond 2500 nm: 6 → 4 at 2626 nm, 5 → 4 at 4052 nm, 7 → 5 at 4654 nm, 6 → 5 at 7460 nm and 7 → 6 at 12372 nm. The sim marks them with an arrow and a count at the right edge, and the readout still gives the true wavelength.

The model has other limits. The atom view spaces the rings evenly so every jump stays watchable, but the true Bohr radii grow as n². Real hydrogen has levels beyond n = 7, so each series bunches towards a limit: 91 nm for Lyman, 365 nm for Balmer and 821 nm for Paschen. The Bohr orbits themselves are a picture. Quantum mechanics replaces them, but it gives the same line wavelengths.

See itFire the jump 7 → 5. Watch for: no line on the strip, an arrow at the right edge, and a readout of about 4654 nm.
08

Where it matters

  • Glowing nebulae. The red light of the 3 → 2 line, at 656 nm, gives clouds of hot hydrogen their red colour, so photographs of nebulae often glow red.
  • Identifying stars. Dark Balmer lines in a star's spectrum show that its atmosphere holds hydrogen hot enough for atoms to sit in n = 2.
  • Observing from space. Lyman lines are ultraviolet, and air absorbs this light, so telescopes must work above the atmosphere to record them.
09

Summary

In one line. A jump between two energy levels sends out or takes in one photon, and the size of the gap sets its wavelength.

Key points

  • Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV. The photon has ΔE = E(upper) − E(lower) and λ = hc/ΔE.
  • Series are named by the lower level: Lyman n = 1 (ultraviolet), Balmer n = 2 (visible), Paschen n = 3 (infrared).
  • Absorption of a jump has the same λ as its emission, but needs the atom already in the lower level.

Common mix-ups

  • "Hydrogen's lines are all colours you can see." Only the five Balmer lines are visible. Lyman and Paschen lines are not.
  • "The orbits are drawn to scale." The rings are evenly spaced for clarity. True radii grow as n².
  • "A larger n means a larger jump." Higher levels are closer together, so the gaps shrink as n rises.

Things to try on your own

  • Run the Paschen series and check that all four lines sit right of the visible band.
  • Switch to Absorption and run Lyman. Check that each black line matches an emission line you saw before.
